  "draft_n": "Mr. and Mrs. Shelby, after their protracted discussion of the night before, did not readily sink to repose, and, in consequence, slept somewhat later than usual the ensuing morning.

"I wonder what keeps Eliza," said Mrs. Shelby, after giving her bell repeated pulls, to no purpose.

Mr. Shelby was before his dressing-glass, razor in hand, when the door opened and a colored boy entered with shaving-water.

"Andy," said his mistress, "step to Eliza's door, and tell her I have rung for her three times. Poor thing!" she added, with a sigh.

Andy soon returned, eyes wide.

"Lor, Missis! Lizy's drawers is all open, and her things lyin' every which way; and I b'lieve she's just done clared out!"

The truth flashed on both at once. Mr. Shelby exclaimed,

"Then she suspected it, and she's off!"

"The Lord be thanked!" said Mrs. Shelby. "I trust she is."

"Wife, you talk like a fool! It will be something pretty awkward for me, if she is. Haley saw I hesitated about selling this child; he'll think I connived at it. It touches my honor!" And he left the room hastily.

There was running and ejaculating, doors opened and shut, faces of all shades peered everywhere. One person only, who might have shed light, was silent,—the head cook, Aunt Chloe. With a heavy cloud on her face, she went on making breakfast biscuits, as if she saw and heard nothing.

Soon a flock of little roosters were roosting on the verandah rails, every one bent on being first to apprise the strange Mas'r of his ill luck. There was whispering, winking, and proclamations that "he'll be rael mad, I'll be bound!" mingled with recollections of his swearing yesterday.

When, at last, Haley appeared, booted and spurred, he was saluted with the tidings on every hand; and the imps were not disappointed of their hope to hear him "swar," which he did with a fluency and fervency that delighted them, while they dodged his riding-whip and tumbled in a heap under the verandah, kicking up their heels in immeasurable giggle.

"If I had the little devils!" muttered Haley, between his teeth.

"But you ha'nt got 'em, though!" said Andy, with a flourish and a string of indescribable mouths at the trader's back, once he was beyond hearing.

"I say now, Shelby, this yer's a most extro'rnary business!" said Haley, abruptly entering the parlor. "It seems that gal's off, with her young un."

"Mr. Haley, Mrs. Shelby is present," said Mr. Shelby.

"I beg pardon, ma'am," said Haley, bowing with a lowering brow; "but I say this yer's a sing'lar report. Is it true, sir?"

"Sir," said Mr. Shelby, "if you wish to communicate with me, you must observe something of the decorum of a gentleman. Andy, take Mr. Haley's hat and riding-whip. Take a seat, sir. Yes, sir; I regret to say, the young woman, excited by overhearing, or having reported to her, something of this business, has taken her child in the night and made off."

"I did expect fair dealing in this matter," said Haley.

"Well, sir," said Mr. Shelby, turning sharply, "what am I to understand by that remark? If any man calls my honor in question, I have but one answer for him."

The trader cowered a little, and said, lower, "It's plaguy hard on a fellow, that had made a fair bargain, to be gulled that way."

"Mr. Haley," said Mr. Shelby, "if I did not think you had some cause for disappointment, I should not have borne your rude and unceremonious entrance. I allow of no insinuations upon me, as if I were partner to any unfairness. Moreover, I shall give you every assistance, in the use of horses, servants, &c., for the recovery of your property. So, in short, Haley,"—and he dropped to his ordinary easy frankness,—"the best way is to keep good-natured and eat some breakfast, and then we will see what is to be done."

Mrs. Shelby rose, said engagements would prevent her being at table, and, deputing a very respectable mulatto woman to attend the gentlemen's coffee at the sideboard, left the room.

"Old lady don't like your humble servant, over and above," said Haley, with an uneasy attempt at familiarity.

"I am not accustomed to hear my wife spoken of with such freedom," said Mr. Shelby, dryly.

"Beg pardon; of course—only a joke, you know," stammered Haley.

"Some jokes are less agreeable than others," rejoined Shelby.

The rumor of Tom's fate and Eliza's flight went round the place like fire in stubble. It was the topic everywhere; nothing was done but to discuss what would come of it. Black Sam—so called for being some shades blacker than any other son of ebony there—revolved the matter with a comprehensiveness of vision and a strict lookout to his own well-being, that would have done credit to any white patriot in Washington.

"It's an ill wind dat blow nowhar,—dat ar a fact," said Sam, sententiously, giving a hoist to his pantaloons, and adroitly substituting a long nail for a missing suspender-button.

"Yes, it's an ill wind blows nowhar," he repeated. "Now, dar, Tom's down—wal, course der's room for some nigger to be up—and why not dis nigger?—dat's de idee. Tom, a ridin' round—boots blacked—pass in his pocket—all grand as Cuffee—but who he? Now, why shouldn't Sam?—dat's what I want to know."

"Halloo, Sam—O Sam! Mas'r wants you to cotch Bill and Jerry," cried Andy.

"High! what's afoot now, young un?"

"Why, you don't know, I s'pose, that Lizy's cut stick, and clared out, with her young un?"

"You teach your granny!" said Sam, with infinite contempt. "Knows it a heap sight sooner than you did; dis nigger an't so green, now!"

"Well, anyhow, Mas'r wants Bill and Jerry geared; and you and I 's to go with Mas'r Haley, to look arter her."

"Good, now! dat's de time o' day!" said Sam. "It's Sam dat's called for in dese yer times. He's de nigger. See if I don't cotch her, now; Mas'r'll see what Sam can do!"

"Ah! but, Sam," said Andy, "you'd better think twice; for Missis don't want her cotched, and she'll be in yer wool."

"High!" said Sam, opening his eyes. "How you know dat?"

"Heard her say so, my own self, dis blessed mornin', when I bring in Mas'r's shaving-water. She sent me to see why Lizy didn't come; and when I telled her she was off, she jest riz up, and ses she, 'The Lord be praised;' and Mas'r, he seemed rael mad, and ses he, 'Wife, you talk like a fool.' But Lor! she'll bring him to! It's allers best to stand Missis' side o' de fence."

Sam scratched his woolly pate,—which, if it did not contain deep wisdom, held much of that species called "knowing which side the bread is buttered." After a hitch to his pantaloons—his method for assisting perplexities—he delivered himself gravely:

"Der an't no sayin'—never—'bout no kind o' thing in dis yer world," he said at last, emphasizing this like a philosopher, as if he had tried other worlds.

"Now, sartin I'd a said Missis would a scoured de varsal world after Lizy," added Sam, thoughtfully.

"So she would," said Andy; "but can't ye see through a ladder, ye black nigger? Missis don't want dis yer Mas'r Haley to get Lizy's boy; dat's de go!"

"High!" said Sam, with that indescribable intonation born of his race.

"And ye'd best be makin' tracks for dem hosses,—mighty sudden,—for I hearn Missis 'quirin' arter yer," added Andy.

Sam bestirred himself; and soon came bearing down gloriously with Bill and Jerry in a full canter; adroitly throwing himself off, he brought them up at the horse-post like a tornado. Haley's horse, a skittish young colt, winced and pulled hard.

"Ho, ho! skeery, ar ye?" said Sam, a mischievous gleam lighting his black visage. "I'll fix ye now!"

Under the beech that overshadowed the place, the small sharp triangular beech-nuts lay thick. With one between finger and thumb, Sam approached the colt, stroking and soothing; and, on pretence of adjusting the saddle, slipped under it the little torment, so that the least weight would fret the animal's nerves without leaving mark.

"Dar!" he said, rolling his eyes with approving grin; "me fix 'em!"

Mrs. Shelby appeared on the balcony, beckoning. Sam approached with as good a determination to pay court as ever suitor at St. James' or Washington.

"Why have you been loitering so, Sam? I sent Andy to hurry you."

"Lord bless you, Missis! horses won't be cotched all in a minnit; they'd done clared out to de south pasture, and the Lord knows whar!"

"Sam, how often must I tell you not to say 'Lord bless you,' and 'the Lord knows,' and such things? It's wicked."

"O, Lord bless my soul! I done forgot, Missis! I won't say nothing of de sort no more."

"Why, Sam, you just have said it again."

"Did I? O, Lord! I mean—I didn't go fur to say it."

"You must be careful, Sam."

"Just let me get my breath, Missis, and I'll start fair. I'll be bery careful."

"Well, Sam, you are to go with Mr. Haley, to show him the road, and help him. Be careful of the horses; you know Jerry was a little lame last week; don't ride them too fast."

Mrs. Shelby spoke the last words low, with strong emphasis.

"Let dis child alone for dat!" said Sam, rolling up his eyes with a volume of meaning. "Lord knows! High!—didn't say dat!"—and he caught his breath with such a ludicrous flourish that his mistress laughed, spite of herself. "Yes, Missis, I'll look out for de hosses!"

"Now, Andy," said Sam, under the beech, "I wouldn't be 't all surprised if dat gen'lman's crittur should gib a fling, by and by. You know, Andy, critturs will do such things;"—and Sam poked him, suggestive.

"High!" said Andy, with instant appreciation.

"Yes; Missis wants to make time,—dat ar's clar. I jis make a little for her. Now, you see, get all dese yer hosses loose, caperin' permiscus, and I spec Mas'r won't be off in a hurry."

Andy grinned.

"Yer see," said Sam, "if Mas'r Haley's horse should begin to act contrary, and cut up, you and I jist lets go of our'n to help him, and we'll help him—oh yes!" They threw back their heads and broke into a low, immoderate laugh, snapping fingers and flourishing heels with exquisite delight.

Haley appeared on the verandah, somewhat mollified by cups of very good coffee; he came out smiling and talking. Sam and Andy, clawing for fragmentary palm-leaves they were pleased to call hats, flew to the horse-posts.

"Well, boys," said Haley, "look alive now; we must lose no time."

"Not a bit of him, Mas'r!" said Sam, putting the rein in his hand and holding his stirrup, while Andy untied Bill and Jerry.

The instant Haley touched the saddle, the mettlesome creature bounded with a spring that threw his master sprawling on the soft turf. Sam, with frantic ejaculations, made a dive at the reins, but only succeeded in brushing his blazing palm-leaf into the horse's eyes, which did not allay his confusion. Over went Sam; the white beast, with snorts and whisking heels, pranced away toward the lower lawn, followed by Bill and Jerry, whom Andy had not failed to let loose, speeding them off with direful cries.

Now ensued a miscellaneous scene of confusion. Sam and Andy ran and shouted,—dogs barked here and there,—and all the smaller specimens on the place, male and female, raced, clapped hands, whooped, and shouted with outrageous officiousness. The white horse, fleet and spirited, entered into the sport with gusto; having a lawn of near half a mile, sloping into indefinite woodland, he took delight in letting pursuers come near, then whisking off with a snort, and careered far down some alley of the wood-lot.

Nothing was further from Sam's mind than to have any one of the troop taken until the season should seem to him most befitting; and the exertions that he made were certainly most heroic. Like the sword of Coeur de Lion, always blazing in the thickest of the battle, Sam's palm-leaf was to be seen everywhere when there was the least danger that a horse could be caught; there he would bear down, shouting, "Now for it! cotch him! cotch him!" in a way to set everything to rout.

Haley ran up and down, cursed, swore, and stamped miscellaneously. Mr. Shelby in vain shouted directions from the balcony; and Mrs. Shelby from her chamber window alternately laughed and wondered,—not without some inkling of what lay at the bottom.

At last, about twelve o'clock, Sam appeared triumphant, mounted on Jerry, with Haley's horse by his side, reeking with sweat, but with flashing eyes and dilated nostrils, as if the spirit of freedom had not yet quite subsided.

"He's cotched!" he exclaimed, triumphantly. "If 't hadn't been for me, they might a bust themselves, all on 'em; but I cotched him!"

"You!" growled Haley, in no amiable mood. "If it hadn't been for you, this never would have happened."

"Lord bless us, Mas'r," said Sam, in the deepest concern, "and me that has been racin' and chasin' till the sweat pours!"

"Well, well!" said Haley, "you've lost me near three hours, with your cursed nonsense. Now let's be off, and have no more fooling."

"Why, Mas'r," said Sam, deprecating, "I b'lieve you mean to kill us all clar, horses and all. Here we is ready to drop, and de critters in a reek. Mas'r won't think o' startin' now till arter dinner. Mas'r's hoss wants rubben down; see how he splashed hisself; and Jerry limps too; don't think Missis would be willin' we should start dis yer way, no how. Lord bless you, Mas'r, we can ketch up, if we do stop. Lizy never was no great walker."

Mrs. Shelby, who, greatly to her amusement, had overheard, now resolved to do her part. She came forward, courteously expressed concern for Haley's accident, and pressed him to stay to dinner, saying the cook should bring it on immediately.

All things considered, Haley, with rather an equivocal grace, proceeded to the parlor; while Sam, rolling his eyes after him with unutterable meaning, led the horses to the stable-yard.

"Did yer see him, Andy? did yer see him?" said Sam, once beyond the barn, fastening the horse. "O, Lor, if it warn't as good as a meetin', to see him a dancin' and kickin' and swarin' at us. 'Swar away, ole fellow,' says I to myself; 'will yer have yer hoss now, or wait till you cotch him?' Lor, Andy, I think I can see him now."

"Yer oughter seen how mad he looked, when you brought de hoss up. Lord, he'd a killed you, if he durs' to; and there you was a standin' as innercent and humble," said Andy.

"Rather specks I am an old hoss," said Sam. "Did yer see Missis up stars at de winder? I seed her laughin'."

"I was racin' so, I didn't see nothing," said Andy.

"Well, yer see," said Sam, proceeding gravely to wash down Haley's pony, "I 'se 'quired what yer may call a habit o' bobservation, Andy. It's a very 'portant habit; and I 'commend yer to be cultivatin' it, now yer young. Hist up dat hind foot. Yer see, Andy, it's bobservation makes all de difference in niggers. Didn't I see which way de wind blew dis yer mornin'? Didn't I see what Missis wanted, though she never let on? Dat ar's bobservation. I 'spects it's what you may call a faculty. Faculties is different in different peoples, but cultivation goes a great way."

"I guess if I hadn't helped your bobservation dis mornin', yer wouldn't have seen your way so smart," said Andy.

"Andy," said Sam, "you's a promisin' child, der an't no manner o' doubt. I thinks lots o' yer; and I don't feel no ways ashamed to take idees from you. We oughtenter overlook nobody, 'cause de smartest on us gets tripped up sometimes. And so, Andy, let's go up to de house now. I'll be boun' Missis'll give us an uncommon good bite, dis yer time."",
  "draft_np1": "The Mother's Struggle

It is impossible to conceive of a human creature more wholly desolate and forlorn than Eliza, when she turned her footsteps from Uncle Tom's cabin.

Her husband's suffering, the danger of her child, the risk she ran in leaving the only home she had ever known, in cutting loose from a friend whom she loved and revered—all blended in a confused and stunning sense; and the parting from every familiar object, the trees under which she had played, the groves where she had walked by the side of her young husband, lay in the clear, frosty starlight and seemed to ask reproachfully whither she could go from a home like that.

But stronger than all was maternal love, wrought into a paroxysm of frenzy by the near approach of fearful danger. Her boy was old enough to have walked by her side, but the bare thought of putting him out of her arms made her shudder, and she strained him to her bosom with a convulsive grasp, as she went rapidly forward.

The frosty ground creaked beneath her feet, and she trembled at the sound; every quaking leaf and fluttering shadow sent the blood backward to her heart. She wondered at the strength that seemed to be come upon her; for she felt the weight of her boy as if it had been a feather, and from her pale lips burst forth, in frequent ejaculations, the prayer to a Friend above—"Lord, help! Lord, save me!"

If it were _your_ Harry, mother, or your Willie, that were going to be torn from you by a brutal trader, tomorrow morning,—if you had seen the man, and heard that the papers were signed and delivered, and you had only from twelve o'clock till morning to make good your escape,—how fast could _you_ walk? How many miles could you make in those few brief hours, with the darling at your bosom,—the little sleepy head on your shoulder,—the small, soft arms trustingly holding on to your neck?

For the child slept. His mother so hurriedly repressed every breath, and so assured him that if he were only still she would certainly save him, that he clung quietly round her neck, only asking, as he found himself sinking to sleep,

"Mother, I don't need to keep awake, do I?"

"No, my darling; sleep, if you want to."

"But, mother, if I do get asleep, you won't let him get me?"

"No! so may God help me!" said his mother, with a paler cheek, and a brighter light in her large dark eyes.

"You're _sure_, an't you, mother?"

"Yes, _sure_!" said the mother, in a voice that startled herself; for it seemed to come from a spirit within, that was no part of her. The boy dropped his weary head on her shoulder, and was soon asleep. How the touch of those warm arms, the gentle breathings that came in her neck, seemed to add fire and spirit to her movements! Sublime is the dominion of the mind over the body, that, for a time, can string the sinews like steel, so that the weak become so mighty.

The boundaries of the farm passed by her dizzily, and still she went, leaving one familiar object after another, slacking not, pausing not, till reddening daylight found her many a long mile from any familiar object on the open highway.

She had often visited connections in the little village of T——, not far from the Ohio river, with her mistress, and knew the road well. To go thither, to escape across the Ohio, were the first hurried outlines of her plan; beyond that, she could only hope in God.

When horses and vehicles began to move along the highway, she became aware that her headlong pace and distracted air might bring on her remark and suspicion. She therefore put the boy on the ground, and, adjusting her dress and bonnet, walked on at as rapid a pace as she thought consistent with appearances. In her bundle she had cakes and apples, which she used to quicken the child—rolling an apple some yards before them, and the boy would run after it with all his might; this ruse, often repeated, carried them many a half-mile.

After a while they came to a thick patch of woodland, through which murmured a clear brook. As the child complained of hunger and thirst, she sat behind a large rock and gave him a breakfast out of her little package. The boy wondered that she could not eat; and when, putting his arms round her neck, he tried to wedge some of his cake into her mouth, the rising in her throat seemed to choke her.

"No, no, Harry darling! mother can't eat till you are safe! We must go on—on—till we come to the river!"

She was many miles past any neighborhood where she was known. Her white skin and the boy's let her pass without a critical survey. At noon she stopped at a neat farmhouse to rest and buy dinner, and the kindly, gossipping woman accepted Eliza's statement that she "was going on a little piece, to spend a week with her friends,"—all which she hoped in her heart might prove strictly true.

An hour before sunset she entered the village of T—— by the Ohio, weary and foot-sore, but still strong in heart. Her first glance was at the river, which lay, like Jordan, between her and the Canaan of liberty on the other side.

It was now early spring, and the river was swollen and turbulent; great cakes of floating ice were swinging heavily to and fro in the turbid waters. Owing to the peculiar form of the Kentucky shore, the ice had been lodged and detained in great quantities, and the narrow channel which swept round the bend was full of ice piled one cake over another, forming a great, undulating raft, filling up the whole river.

Eliza saw at once that the ferry-boat could not run, and turned into a small public house on the bank. The hostess, busy with a fork in her hand, stopped as Eliza's sweet and plaintive voice arrested her.

"Isn't there any ferry or boat, that takes people over to B——, now?"

"No, indeed!" said the woman; "the boats has stopped running. May be you're wanting to get over?—anybody sick? Ye seem mighty anxious?"

"I've got a child that's very dangerous," said Eliza. "I never heard of it till last night, and I've walked quite a piece today, in hopes to get to the ferry."

"Well, now, that's onlucky," said the woman, whose motherly sympathies were much aroused. She called to a man at the back, who appeared in a leather apron, and learned that a neighbor down the road was going over with some truck that evening, if he durs'd. "He'll be in here to supper tonight; you'd better set down and wait."

The child was wholly exhausted. Eliza laid the weary boy upon a comfortable bed in a small bed-room, and held his hands in hers till he was fast asleep. For her there was no rest. As a fire in her bones, the thought of the pursuer urged her on; and she gazed with longing eyes on the sullen, surging waters that lay between her and liberty.

Here we must take our leave of her for the present, to follow the course of her pursuers.

Though Mrs. Shelby had promised that the dinner should be hurried on table, it was soon seen that it required more than one to make a bargain. The order was fairly given out in Haley's hearing, but Aunt Chloe only gave certain very gruff snorts, and tosses of her head, and went on with every operation in an unusually leisurely and circumstantial manner.

For some singular reason, an impression seemed to reign among the servants generally that Missis would not be particularly disobliged by delay; and a wonderful number of counter accidents occurred. One luckless wight upset the gravy, which had to be got up _de novo_, Aunt Chloe answering shortly that she "warn't a going to have raw gravy on the table, to help nobody's catchings." Another tumbled with the water; another precipitated the butter; and giggling news came that "Mas'r Haley was mighty oneasy, and couldn't sit in his cheer no ways, but was a walkin' and stalkin' to the winders and through the porch."

"Sarves him right!" said Aunt Chloe, indignantly. "He'll get wus nor oneasy, one of these days. _His_ master'll be sending for him, and then see how he'll look! He's broke a many, many, many hearts,—I tell ye all!" she said, stopping with a fork uplifted; "it's like what Mas'r George reads in Ravelations,—souls a callin' under the altar! and a callin' on the Lord for vengeance on sich!—and by and by the Lord he'll hear 'em—so he will!"

"He'll go to torment, and no mistake," said little Jake.

"Sich'll be burnt up forever, and no mistake; won't ther?" said Andy.

"Chil'en!" said a voice that made them all start. It was Uncle Tom, who had come in, and stood listening to the conversation at the door. "Chil'en! I'm afeard you don't know what ye're sayin'. Forever is a _dre'ful_ word, chil'en; it's awful to think on 't. You oughtenter wish that ar to any human crittur."

"Don't natur herself kinder cry out on 'em?" said Aunt Chloe. "Don't dey tear der suckin' baby right off his mother's breast, and sell him, and der little children as is crying and holding on by her clothes,—don't dey pull 'em off and sells 'em? Don't dey tear wife and husband apart?" said Aunt Chloe, beginning to cry, "when it's jest takin' the very life on 'em? Lor, if the devil don't get them, what's he good for?" And Aunt Chloe covered her face with her checked apron, and began to sob in good earnest.

"Pray for them that 'spitefully use you, the good book says," said Tom.

"Pray for 'em!" said Aunt Chloe; "Lor, it's too tough! I can't pray for 'em."

"It's natur, Chloe, and natur 's strong," said Tom, "but the Lord's grace is stronger; you oughter think what an awful state a poor crittur's soul 's in that'll do them ar things. I'd rather be sold, ten thousand times over, than to have all that ar poor crittur's got to answer for."

The bell rang, and Tom was summoned to the parlor.

"Tom," said his master, kindly, "I want you to notice that I give this gentleman bonds to forfeit a thousand dollars if you are not on the spot when he wants you; he's going today to look after his other business, and you can have the day to yourself. Go anywhere you like, boy."

"Thank you, Mas'r," said Tom.

"And mind yourself," said the trader, "and don't come it over your master with any o' yer nigger tricks; for I'll take every cent out of him, if you an't thar."

"Mas'r," said Tom,—and he stood very straight,—"I was jist eight years old when ole Missis put you into my arms, and you wasn't a year old. 'Thar,' says she, 'Tom, that's to be _your_ young Mas'r; take good care on him,' says she. And now I jist ask you, Mas'r, have I ever broke word to you, or gone contrary to you, 'specially since I was a Christian?"

Mr. Shelby was fairly overcome, and the tears rose to his eyes.

"My good boy, the Lord knows you say but the truth; and if I was able to help it, all the world shouldn't buy you."

"And sure as I am a Christian woman," said Mrs. Shelby, "you shall be redeemed as soon as I can any way bring together means. Sir," she said to Haley, "take good account of who you sell him to, and let me know."

"Lor, yes, for that matter," said the trader, "I may bring him up in a year, not much the wuss for wear, and trade him back."

"I'll trade with you then, and make it for your advantage," said Mrs. Shelby.

Mr. and Mrs. Shelby both felt annoyed and degraded by the familiar impudence of the trader, yet saw the absolute necessity of putting a constraint on their feelings. The more hopelessly sordid he appeared, the greater became Mrs. Shelby's dread of his recapturing Eliza, and the greater her motive for detaining him by every female artifice. She therefore graciously smiled, assented, and did all she could to make time pass imperceptibly.

At two o'clock Sam and Andy brought the horses up to the posts, apparently greatly refreshed by the scamper of the morning.

"Your master, I s'pose, don't keep no dogs," said Haley, as he prepared to mount.

"Heaps on 'em," said Sam, triumphantly; "thar's Bruno—he's a roarer!"

"Poh!" said Haley. "But your master don't keep no dogs for trackin' out niggers."

Sam knew exactly what he meant, but kept on a look of earnest and desperate simplicity. "Our dogs all smells round considable sharp. They's _far_ dogs at most anything, if you'd get 'em started."

"You go hang!" said Haley. "Come, tumble up now."

"I shall take the straight road to the river," said Haley, when they had come to the boundaries of the estate. "I know the way of all of 'em,—they makes tracks for the underground."

"Sartin," said Sam, "dat's de idee. Now, der's two roads to de river,—de dirt road and der pike,—which Mas'r mean to take?"

Andy looked up innocently at Sam, surprised at hearing this new geographical fact, but instantly confirmed what he said by a vehement reiteration.

"'Cause," said Sam, "I'd rather be 'clined to 'magine that Lizy 'd take de dirt road, bein' it's the least travelled."

Haley, notwithstanding that he was a very old bird, was rather brought up by this view of the case. "If yer warn't both on yer such cussed liars, now!" he said contemplatively.

The pensive tone amused Andy prodigiously, while Sam's face was immovably composed into the most doleful gravity.

"Course," said Sam, "Mas'r can do as he'd ruther. Now, when I study 'pon it, I think de straight road de best, _deridedly_."

"She would naturally go a lonesome way," said Haley, thinking aloud.

"Dar an't no sayin'," said Sam; "gals is pecular; they never does nothin' ye thinks they will; mose gen'lly the contrary. Now, my private 'pinion is, Lizy took der road; so I think we'd better take de straight one."

This profound generic view did not dispose Haley to the straight road, and he announced he should go the other.

"Now I think on 't, I think I hearn 'em tell that dat ar road was all fenced up and down by der creek, and thar, an't it, Andy?"

Andy was strictly noncommittal.

Haley, accustomed to strike the balance between lies of greater or lesser magnitude, thought that it lay in favor of the dirt road. The mention of the thing he thought he perceived was involuntary on Sam's part at first, and his confused attempts to dissuade he set down to a desperate lying on second thoughts. When Sam indicated the road, Haley plunged briskly into it.

The road, in fact, was an old one, abandoned for many years after the laying of the new pike. It was open for about an hour's ride, and after that cut across by various farms and fences. Sam knew this perfectly well; Andy had never heard of it. He rode along with an air of dutiful submission, only groaning that 't was "desp't rough, and bad for Jerry's foot."

"Now, I jest give yer warning," said Haley, "I know yer; yer won't get me to turn off this road, with all yer fussin'—so you shet up!"

"Mas'r will go his own way!" said Sam, with rueful submission, winking most portentously to Andy.

Sam was in wonderful spirits—at one time exclaiming that he saw "a gal's bonnet" on the top of some distant eminence, or calling to Andy "if that thar wasn't 'Lizy' down in the hollow"; always making these exclamations in some rough or craggy part of the road, where the sudden quickening of speed was a special inconvenience to all parties concerned, and thus keeping Haley in a state of constant commotion.

After riding about an hour, the whole party made a precipitate and tumultuous descent into a barn-yard belonging to a large farming establishment. Not a soul was in sight; and as the barn stood plainly square across the road, it was evident their journey in that direction had reached a decided finale.

"Wan't dat ar what I telled Mas'r?" said Sam, with an air of injured innocence. "How does strange gentleman spect to know more about a country dan de natives born and raised?"

"You rascal!" said Haley, "you knew all about this."

"Didn't I tell yer I _knowd_, and yer wouldn't believe me? I telled Mas'r 't was all shet up, and fenced up, and I didn't spect we could get through,—Andy heard me."

It was all too true to be disputed, and the unlucky man had to pocket his wrath, and all three faced about for the highway.

In consequence of all the various delays, it was about three-quarters of an hour after Eliza had laid her child to sleep that the party came riding into the same village. Eliza was standing by the window, looking out in another direction, when Sam's quick eye caught a glimpse of her. At this crisis, Sam contrived to have his hat blown off, and uttered a loud and characteristic ejaculation, which startled her at once; she drew suddenly back; the whole train swept by the window, round to the front door.

A thousand lives seemed to be concentrated in that one moment to Eliza. Her room opened by a side door to the river. She caught her child, and sprang down the steps towards it. The trader caught a full glimpse of her just as she was disappearing down the bank; and throwing himself from his horse, and calling loudly on Sam and Andy, he was after her like a hound after a deer. In that dizzy moment her feet to her scarce seemed to touch the ground, and a moment brought her to the water's edge. Right on behind they came; and, nerved with strength such as God gives only to the desperate, with one wild cry and flying leap, she vaulted sheer over the turbid current by the shore, on to the raft of ice beyond. It was a desperate leap—impossible to anything but madness and despair; and Haley, Sam, and Andy, instinctively cried out, and lifted up their hands, as she did it.

The huge green fragment of ice on which she alighted pitched and creaked as her weight came on it, but she staid there not a moment. With wild cries and desperate energy she leaped to another and still another cake; stumbling—leaping—slipping—springing upwards again! Her shoes are gone—her stockings cut from her feet—while blood marked every step; but she saw nothing, felt nothing, till dimly, as in a dream, she saw the Ohio side, and a man helping her up the bank.

"Yer a brave gal, now, whoever ye ar!" said the man, with an oath.

Eliza recognized the voice and face for a man who owned a farm not far from her old home.

"O, Mr. Symmes!—save me—do save me—do hide me!" said Eliza.

"Why, what's this?" said the man. "Why, if 'tan't Shelby's gal!"

"My child!—this boy!—he'd sold him! There is his Mas'r," said she, pointing to the Kentucky shore. "O, Mr. Symmes, you've got a little boy!"

"So I have," said the man, as he roughly, but kindly, drew her up the steep bank. "Besides, you're a right brave gal. I like grit, wherever I see it."

When they had gained the top of the bank, the man paused. "I'd be glad to do something for ye; but then there's nowhar I could take ye. The best I can do is to tell ye to go _thar_," said he, pointing to a large white house which stood by itself, off the main street. "Go thar; they're kind folks. Thar's no kind o' danger but they'll help you,—they're up to all that sort o' thing."

"The Lord bless you!" said Eliza, earnestly.

"No 'casion, no 'casion in the world. Come, now, go along like a likely, sensible gal, as you are. You've arnt your liberty, and you shall have it, for all me."

The woman folded her child to her bosom, and walked firmly and swiftly away. The man stood and looked after her.

"Shelby, now, mebbe won't think this yer the most neighborly thing in the world; but what's a feller to do? Somehow I never could see no kind o' critter a strivin' and pantin', and trying to clar theirselves, with the dogs arter 'em and go agin 'em. Besides, I don't see no kind of 'casion for me to be hunter and catcher for other folks, neither."

So spoke this poor, heathenish Kentuckian, who had not been instructed in his constitutional relations, and consequently was betrayed into acting in a sort of Christianized manner, which, if he had been better situated and more enlightened, he would not have been left to do.

Haley had stood a perfectly amazed spectator till Eliza had disappeared up the bank, when he turned a blank, inquiring look on Sam and Andy.

"That ar was a tolable fair stroke of business," said Sam.

"The gal 's got seven devils in her, I believe!" said Haley. "How like a wildcat she jumped!"

"Wal, now," said Sam, scratching his head, "I hope Mas'r'll 'scuse us trying dat ar road. Don't think I feel spry enough for dat ar, no way!" and Sam gave a hoarse chuckle.

"_You_ laugh!" said the trader, with a growl.

"Lord bless you, Mas'r, I couldn't help it now," said Sam, giving way to the long pent-up delight of his soul. "She looked so curi's, a leapin' and springin'—ice a crackin'—and only to hear her,—plump! ker chunk! ker splash! Spring! Lord! how she goes it!" and Sam and Andy laughed till the tears rolled down their cheeks.

"I'll make ye laugh t' other side yer mouths!" said the trader, laying about their heads with his riding-whip.

Both ducked, and ran shouting up the bank, and were on their horses before he was up.

"Good-evening, Mas'r!" said Sam, with much gravity. "I berry much spect Missis be anxious 'bout Jerry. Mas'r Haley won't want us no longer. Missis wouldn't hear of our ridin' the critters over Lizy's bridge tonight"; and, with a facetious poke into Andy's ribs, he started off, followed by the latter, at full speed,—their shouts of laughter coming faintly on the wind."
